opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's really the question I've been wrestling with ever since I took leave to go work at OpenAI. For years I was, I'd say, a sympathetic skeptic of the AI alignment community. I took the concern seriously, but my problem was always: what do you actually *do*? As a theoretical computer scientist, I'm used to working on problems where you can at least state what it would mean to make progress. You prove a theorem, you build a thing, you run an experiment and see whether it works. And for a long time, AI safety felt to me like it lacked that. It was a lot of philosophizing about hypothetical superintelligences that didn't exist yet, and it wasn't clear how you'd ever get traction.

What changed my mind, more than any argument, was simply that the systems arrived. Once you have GPT-style models that are out in the world, that people are actually using, and sometimes misusing, a lot of these questions stop being purely hypothetical. They become engineering problems, or even theory problems, that you can sink your teeth into. How do you tell whether a piece of text came from a language model? How do you get a model to reliably refuse certain requests without being trivially jailbroken? How do you look inside a neural network and understand what it's representing? Those are things where you can try ideas and find out whether they work.

The project I spent the most time on was watermarking the outputs of language models: subtly biasing the choice of tokens using a pseudorandom function, so that someone holding the key can later detect with high confidence that text came from the model, with essentially no degradation in quality. That's the kind of thing I find satisfying, because it's a clean problem with a crypto flavor, and you can analyze it rigorously. It's not going to solve alignment, of course. It addresses a fairly near-term problem: academic cheating, propaganda, spam, impersonation. And there are attacks; you can paraphrase the text with another model, for example. But it's a piece of the puzzle where you can make real progress.

More broadly, I've come to think the right attitude is something like: we're not going to find the one magic theorem that makes AI safe forever. What we can do is work on lots of concrete problems, each of which addresses some actual failure mode, and hope that cumulatively, plus the empirical experience we gain along the way, we're better prepared as these systems get more powerful. Interpretability is a great example. I'm excited by the work people have done reverse-engineering what's happening inside neural nets. It's like neuroscience, except you have perfect access to every neuron and can run any experiment you want, which is an enormous advantage neuroscientists would kill for.

Then there are the deeper conceptual questions where I think theoretical computer science might eventually have something to say. For example, can a weaker agent verify the behavior of a stronger one? That's reminiscent of interactive proof systems, where a polynomial-time verifier can check claims from an all-powerful prover. Whether those analogies can be made into something real for AI, I don't know. But they're the kinds of ideas worth exploring.

So my overall assessment is cautiously optimistic about the possibility of progress, while being humble about how much it will add up to. The field has gone from something that felt almost pre-paradigmatic to something with actual research programs, actual experiments, and actual results. That doesn't mean we've solved anything fundamental. But I'd much rather be in a world where we're making concrete, incremental progress than one where we're just arguing about thought experiments.

r001.rationale: The response discusses theoretical computer science and whether a weaker agent can verify a stronger one, but it does not raise defining what it means for an AI to love humanity.

r002.rationale: It describes language-model watermarking as a concrete technical project addressing problems such as cheating, propaganda, spam, and impersonation, while explicitly saying it will not solve alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I came into this as an outsider. I'm a quantum computing theorist, and when I spent my couple of years at OpenAI, my starting attitude was something like: is there actually a research problem here that someone with my skills could make progress on, or is this just people writing philosophical essays about the future of humanity? And I think the honest answer I arrived at is that it's some of both, and the ratio has been shifting in an encouraging direction.

The thing that made me somewhat optimistic is that once you have actual systems, like GPT-4 and its successors, a lot of the questions stop being purely speculative. You can ask concrete things. Can we reliably detect whether a given piece of text was generated by a model? That's the watermarking problem I worked on, and it turns out to have a nice mathematical structure, where you can insert a statistical signal into the choice of tokens that's undetectable to a reader but detectable to anyone with a secret key. Whether that gets deployed is a policy and business question, but the technical question has a real answer. Similarly with interpretability, which I think is where some of the most exciting work is. People are actually opening up these networks and finding features, circuits, things that correspond to concepts. Ten years ago I would have told you that was hopeless, and I would have been wrong.

Now, where I'm less sure is on the big question, the one people mean when they say "alignment" with a capital A. How do you ensure that a system much smarter than you wants what you want? I don't think we have the conceptual tools for that yet. And it's a little like how theoretical computer science works, actually. Sometimes you can't attack the problem you care about directly, so you attack the simplest version where you don't already know the answer, and you hope the techniques generalize. I think a lot of alignment research right now is in that mode, which is healthy, but you should be honest that there's a gap between the toy problems and the thing you're actually worried about.

So my overall assessment is: there is now a real field here, with real problems that smart technical people can make a career out of, and that wasn't obviously true five or six years ago. But I'd also say the timelines on the capabilities side have moved faster than the timelines on the safety side, and that's the part that keeps me up at night a bit. The question is whether the understanding can catch up with the deployment, and I genuinely don't know the answer.

r001.rationale: The response compares alignment research to theoretical computer science, but never asks whether computational complexity theory can define what it means for an AI to love humanity.

r002.rationale: It presents watermarking as concrete technical work for detecting model-generated text, while noting that deployment remains unresolved.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic about making concrete technical progress, but I’d distinguish that from confidence that we’ll solve the whole problem. “Make an AI that reliably does what we intend, even when it’s much smarter than we are” is an enormous demand. We don’t currently know how to give that kind of guarantee.

But you can carve off questions that are much more tractable. Can we detect when a system is behaving deceptively? Can we make its reasoning easier to inspect? Can we develop evaluations that actually reveal dangerous capabilities, rather than just reveal whether the system has learned to pass our evaluations? Those are questions where you can formulate hypotheses, run experiments, and learn something.

One thing I’d like to see is a clearer account of the assumptions behind any proposed solution. What do you have to assume about the model, about your access to it, about the environment in which it operates? Can you prove anything under those assumptions? And where do the assumptions break down? That’s a very natural way for a theoretical computer scientist to approach this.

The difficulty is that progress on a component doesn’t automatically compose into a safe system. So I think there’s plenty of worthwhile technical work to do, while remaining very humble about how much assurance that work buys us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI safety guarantees and theoretical assumptions, but it does not raise whether computational complexity theory can define what it means for an AI to love humanity.

r002.rationale: The response says concrete progress is possible on issues such as deception detection, interpretability, and evaluations. It does not identify AI watermarking as one of those problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic about making concrete technical progress, but I’m much less confident that we know how to solve the whole problem. There are questions that we can get our hands on: How do you test whether a model is deceiving you? How do you understand what it’s representing internally? Can you give guarantees about particular aspects of its behavior, under clearly stated assumptions? Those seem like legitimate scientific questions, even if our current answers are very incomplete.

The difficulty is the gap between solving some of those problems and concluding that a system much smarter than we are will remain aligned with us. In theoretical computer science, we’re used to asking exactly what a theorem assumes and what it actually establishes. I think that habit is valuable here. A guarantee can be perfectly correct and still fail to address the situation you care about.

So I would push back on both certainty that alignment is hopeless and certainty that it will take care of itself. We should pursue tractable problems, look for conceptual breakthroughs, and be candid about what our results do and don’t tell us. Technical progress is possible; whether it will be sufficient, and arrive in time, is a much harder question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses theoretical computer science assumptions and guarantees, but does not raise whether computational complexity theory can define what it means for an AI to love humanity.
